title: Eighteen Days of War
subtitle: The opening campaign’s victories, surviving Soviet armies, and the consequences of occupation
author: Robert M. Dobo
summary: By 9 July, German armies had shattered the frontier deployment and reached a new defensive region. Their successes concealed a strategic miscalculation: Soviet armies continued to form, while occupation and captivity were already producing mass violence.
body:
On 8 July 1941, the German army's senior leadership presented Hitler with a reassuring calculation. Of 164 Soviet rifle divisions identified so far, eighty-nine were assessed as destroyed, forty-six remained available for commitment, eighteen were assigned to secondary theatres and the whereabouts of eleven were unknown. The categories made a vast and confusing campaign appear countable. They also contained the danger in Germany's interpretation of its victories: the number of formations identified by German intelligence was being treated as a guide to how much resistance the Soviet state could still produce. The figures recorded an assessment, not an independently verified balance sheet of the Red Army.[1]

By 9 July, the eighteenth calendar day of the invasion, the three German army groups faced distinct unfinished battles. In the north, the advance had reached Pskov. In the centre, another Soviet concentration stood across the approaches to Smolensk. In the south, Soviet armies were still withdrawing and threatening the invader’s flanks. The German victories were immense, but the calculation presented to Hitler could not answer the decisive question: how much further organized resistance could the Soviet state produce? This closing study weighs the opening campaign against that uncertainty and against the conditions already imposed on people who had fallen into German hands. [2] [3] [1]

Eighteen days and several different fronts

The eighteen calendar dates from 22 June through 9 July contain several overlapping operations, each with its own tempo. Forward tank formations moved while infantry completed encirclements, artillery repositioned and repair and supply units worked along increasingly extended routes. Some Soviet troops were escaping earlier pockets as fresh formations entered the next battle. These activities make the army’s depth as important as the position of its leading elements. A rate of advance calculated from the frontier to a spearhead measures one aspect of movement, while leaving unanswered how much fighting power could be assembled at that point and how securely its connections could be maintained.[4]

The German situation sheet for 9 July displays that unevenness. The central spearheads reached the Vitebsk and Dnieper approaches while numerous infantry formations remained farther west. In the south, German positions formed a different pattern around the routes toward Kiev, Berdichev and the older Soviet frontier. Along the Romanian wing the fighting still belonged to the campaign through Bessarabia and northern Bukovina. These were not equivalent distances along parallel lanes. Rivers, roads, the distribution of Soviet armies and the choices made by both commands gave each theatre its own operational rhythm.[4]

Scattered Soviet elements still appeared behind the German formations on the 9 July sheet. Their presence mattered operationally: supply routes crossed a rear area that could not simply be treated as empty. The symbols identify the German headquarters’ assessment, preserved in a 1942 compilation; they cannot account for every soldier or village. Soviet orders and reports help restore the other side of that picture, including formations withdrawing or reassembling beyond German observation. [4] [5]

The most useful comparison is therefore between each army group's actual situation and its documented task. Army Group North had to destroy Soviet forces in the Baltic region and advance toward Leningrad. Army Group Centre had to destroy the western Soviet concentration and create the conditions for further operations beyond the Dvina–Dnieper region. Army Group South had to defeat the forces in western Ukraine and prevent an effective withdrawal across the Dnieper. Capturing ground contributed to those tasks, but possession of ground and destruction of the opposing army were not interchangeable achievements.[1]

The northern advance reaches Pskov

Wilhelm Ritter von Leeb's Army Group North had moved far beyond its initial crossings from East Prussia. Erich Hoepner's 4th Panzer Group supplied the mobile lead, while Ernst Busch's 16th Army and Georg von Küchler's 18th Army followed on different axes. The capture of the Western Dvina crossings had disrupted Soviet efforts to make that river a stable barrier. Pskov fell on 9 July, bringing the invasion into another important communications centre on the approach toward Leningrad. The occupation date is confirmed by the city's regional research library as well as the campaign's established chronology.[6][3]

This progress fulfilled an important part of the opening operational purpose: Soviet defence in the Baltic border region had failed to hold the invasion near its starting line. It did not mean that Leningrad was already isolated or that every Soviet formation between the Baltic coast and the central sector had been eliminated. The northern army group still had to carry its infantry forward, protect its flanks and operate through terrain in which roads and crossings channelled movement. German planning in early July explicitly anticipated further resistance near the old Soviet–Estonian frontier and distinguished the panzer group's advance from the infantry's work farther west.[1]

The Soviet Northwestern Front was now under Pyotr Sobennikov rather than the commander who had directed the opening border battles, Fyodor Kuznetsov. A surviving order signed by Sobennikov and his chief of staff, Nikolai Vatutin, at Pskov on 5 July reveals their immediate concerns. Commanders were losing contact with subordinate units and higher headquarters. The order demanded reliable communications, knowledge of neighbouring formations and prompt situation reports. This was a diagnosis of command failure within a continuing military organization, not a declaration that organization had disappeared altogether.[7]

Sobennikov’s proposed response addressed the distribution of force as well as the flow of information. He described German reconnaissance of flanks and formation boundaries, followed by attacks on the weaknesses discovered there. Holding fewer troops continuously along the broad front and assembling small striking groups on likely approaches could, in principle, place a stronger response at the point of danger. The instruction shows a command trying to learn from the manner of its defeats. Its effectiveness would depend on warning, communications and the ability to move those groups in time—the very capabilities whose failure the same order criticized.[7]

The loss of Pskov therefore left the Soviet command with an urgent defensive problem rather than a completed German conquest of the north. Sobennikov’s orders sought to preserve contact and assemble local counterattacks; Leeb’s army group sought to carry the advance toward Lake Ilmen and Leningrad. Whether Soviet formations could act on those orders would determine how much of the next defensive position they could hold. The two commands were already engaged in the next contest, even while Germany counted the successes of the first. [7] [1]

Behind Army Group North’s advancing formations, Riga’s Jewish inhabitants were already being persecuted. On 4 July, Latvian perpetrators set fire to the Great Synagogue with Jews confined inside, as Yad Vashem’s ghetto encyclopaedia records. The burning belonged to the first days of occupation, before the later establishment of the ghetto and the much larger massacres of the autumn. It made the city’s capture a catastrophe for people whose places of worship and refuge had become targets. No precise death toll for this building is used here; the chronology and deliberate killing are the point that the movement of armies alone cannot convey.[8]

The centre faces another Soviet concentration

Army Group Centre had achieved the most spectacular result of the opening period. Fedor von Bock's forces had broken the Soviet Western Front's original deployment and carried out the Białystok–Minsk encirclements. The two panzer groups under Hermann Hoth and Heinz Guderian could now operate far east of the original battlefields. But the conclusion of the main pocket fighting belonged to a process extending into early July. It should not be projected backward onto the capture of Minsk on 28 June, as though the city's fall had simultaneously ended resistance throughout the encircled area.[2][1]

By 9 July, Hoth's forward formations were at Vitebsk and Guderian's at the approaches to the Dnieper. The German map places the 20th Panzer Division and other formations in the Vitebsk sector, while the main Dnieper crossings for the next operation still lay ahead. Smolensk was not yet a conquered city. The immediate German task was to break the defensive region linking Vitebsk, Orsha and Smolensk, opening the corridor farther east. That task required new crossings and new fighting against forces that had not all been inside the earlier pockets.[4][1]

The failed Soviet counterstroke toward Lepel, examined in the 6 July study, made the contrast especially clear. Timoshenko's reconstructed Western Front could place the 5th and 7th Mechanized Corps into action under Kurochkin's 20th Army. It could not make their operations achieve the intended disruption of the German advance. The 5th Corps' report of 9 July described German attacks into the rear of its 17th Tank Division, fragmented withdrawals and incomplete information about subordinate units. Fresh forces had entered the battle, suffered serious setbacks and still left other Soviet armies to be confronted farther east.[5]

The reserve armies were the practical consequence of the mobilization examined in the 3 July study. Their existence overturned the assumption that the forces Germany had identified near the frontier exhausted the Soviet military problem. It did not establish that the new formations would fight effectively: Lepel had already shown how fresh resources could be lost through faulty coordination and disrupted support. For Bock’s command, the immediate consequence was another defended region to break. The need for a new operation was itself evidence that the opening victories had not ended organized resistance. [2]

Army Group Centre had therefore won a major opening campaign and created the opportunity for a second great operation. It had not yet demonstrated that successive operations could be completed before its own strength and support system deteriorated. The distinction was visible without knowledge of the coming winter. The need to force the Dnieper and deal with the reserve armies was already present in German plans. Smolensk represented the next attempt to convert operational momentum into a decision, rather than evidence that the original decision had already been obtained.[1]

The southern armies remain a moving problem

Gerd von Rundstedt's Army Group South had advanced less dramatically than the central group, but its difficulties should not be reduced to a comparison of kilometres. Ewald von Kleist's 1st Panzer Group and Walter von Reichenau's 6th Army had met substantial Soviet armoured counterattacks and persistent resistance on the northern side of their advance. Carl-Heinrich von Stülpnagel's 17th Army operated farther south, while the German 11th Army and Romanian forces widened the offensive from the Prut. Their opponents were distributed across the Southwestern and Southern Fronts, and destroying them required coordination over a much broader and more complicated space.[6][1]

The 9 July German sheet places forward armour around the Zhytomyr–Berdichev approaches, with Soviet concentrations still marked both north and south of the principal thrust. Kiev remained ahead, on the Dnieper. The earlier movement through the Brody–Dubno area had opened routes eastward but had not produced a southern equivalent of the complete central encirclement. A spearhead approaching an important road junction was a real success; it was not proof that the Soviet armies withdrawing on adjacent routes had been caught or that the route behind the spearhead was secure.[4]

Mikhail Kirponos's Southwestern Front continued to pose a connected set of problems. On the northern flank, Mikhail Potapov's 5th Army threatened German communications from the region adjoining the Pripet Marshes. Forces farther south were withdrawing toward older fortified positions and the interior. The German operational reconstruction identifies the 5th Army's pressure as an issue that had to be overcome if 6th Army and 1st Panzer Group were to achieve a decisive result. This was resistance with consequences beyond the immediate ground held: it drew attention and forces toward a flank while the main German purpose required further movement east and south.[1][9]

The argument at Hitler's headquarters on 8 July illustrates the resulting uncertainty. Brauchitsch proposed a relatively close envelopment by 1st Panzer Group, with a protective screen west of Kiev. Hitler preferred taking Kiev first and then attempting a wider operation east of the Dnieper with assistance from Army Group Centre. Brauchitsch objected that the logistical demands of that wider scheme were then prohibitive. No immediate decision settled the dispute. Germany had considerable freedom to choose its next operation, but different commanders disagreed over how to turn that freedom into the destruction of the remaining Soviet armies.[1]

Meanwhile, the Prut offensive did not yet amount to the conquest of the entire southern region. The German–Romanian wing was still working through Bessarabia and northern Bukovina toward the Dniester. In the wider design, 11th Army's movement northeastward was intended to help the operations against Soviet forces in Ukraine. That connection explains why its pace mattered to Rundstedt. It also cautions against treating Romania's immediate territorial aims and Germany's larger encirclement plans as if they were identical tasks completed by the same crossing.[1][4]

Supply that worked under growing strain

The distances already covered made supply a central part of the next operational decisions. German formations needed fuel, ammunition, food, spare parts and replacements, while the infantry and much of its transport still moved at a very different speed from the panzer spearheads. Completing encirclements occupied infantry that would otherwise have been closing up. The German operational study identifies the widening separation between armour and following troops as a danger and stresses the limited number of motorized infantry formations available to bridge it. Rapid movement created opportunities while also enlarging the space that had to be supported and protected.[1]

It would nevertheless be inaccurate to declare that the whole German supply system had already failed on 9 July. The same study judged the early-July arrangements for forward depots and new supply bases adequate for the operations then projected. That assessment was broad and retrospective, and could coexist with acute shortages in individual units. It still matters. A convincing explanation of later difficulties must not be created by assigning them all to the opening fortnight. Germany retained the ability to mount the next major offensive; the question was how long that capacity could be sustained as distances and demands increased.[1]

The railway from Brest toward Minsk illustrates both achievement and limitation. By 3 July, according to the German reconstruction, the track had been converted to the narrower European gauge roughly halfway to Minsk. The remainder reopened two days later using captured Soviet rolling stock. That solution then encountered a specific constraint: the Germans lacked captured Soviet tank cars for carrying fuel. The remaining section consequently also required conversion, allowing German tank cars to operate. A railway line visible on a map was therefore not automatically a functioning fuel route of the required capacity.[1]

For a tank formation, the practical question was when fuel would reach it. Reopening track did not settle that question if the available wagons could not carry petroleum. Conversely, successful conversion and the arrival of German tank cars could restore an essential service. The Brest–Minsk example therefore explains why a functioning supply system could still impose constraints on operational choice. It took labour and scarce transport to keep the advance moving; a more ambitious manoeuvre could demand resources that were not yet available. [1]

The disagreement at Hitler’s headquarters turned this transport problem into a strategic choice. A close envelopment and a wider operation east of the Dnieper did not ask the same things of the supply system. Brauchitsch’s objection concerned the larger demand. German forces could retain the means for a powerful offensive while lacking the immediate support for the most ambitious proposal. Logistics therefore helped define which opportunities were usable, even before shortages became a general explanation for the campaign’s outcome. [1]

The missing tank cars

Blau places the reopening of the unconverted eastern section of the Brest–Minsk railway on 5 July, but dates its subsequent conversion only a few days later. The fuel-tank-car problem is therefore evidence of the developing July supply effort, not proof that every stage had been completed by 9 July. The account’s broad judgment of satisfactory support must be read with that chronological limit. [1]

Counting losses without counting victory twice

The opening intelligence table contained its own warning. Forty-six identified Soviet rifle divisions were assessed as still available, and the whereabouts of eleven more were unknown. Even within Germany’s limited inventory, destruction was not complete. Beyond it lay formations not yet identified and those still being raised. The analytical mistake was to make the impressive destruction of known divisions answer a question the table could not settle: whether the Soviet state could organize another substantial defence. [1]

Prisoner totals require similar care. The Białystok–Minsk operation produced captures on a scale measured in hundreds of thousands, but published totals vary with the boundaries and dates assigned to the operation. Blau reports approximately 290,000, while Ziemke and Bauer describe more than 300,000 for the combined encirclements. These figures should not be silently blended or assigned wholly to 28 June. They describe the accumulated result of the pocket battles, and neither figure represents the number killed in combat. Their scale establishes the disaster without requiring a spurious precision about a single day's captures.[1][2]

A destroyed formation left several kinds of survivors. Some men were prisoners; others were wounded, escaping or already being absorbed into another unit. The Lepel reports show headquarters losing track of subunits without establishing that all their men had been captured. The distinction had practical consequences for rebuilding the Red Army. Returning soldiers could bring experience to new formations, but the guns, vehicles and communications lost with their old units still had to be replaced. [1] [5]

Losses acquire explanatory force when connected to the capacity for the next operation. The Soviet Union’s immense casualties and equipment losses impaired command, mobility and the ability to coordinate supporting arms. German casualties and mechanical wear also affected usable strength, although the army retained powerful offensive capabilities. Neither condition was static: repair, reinforcement, mobilization and further fighting continually changed it. A comparison of cumulative totals must therefore be accompanied by an account of the organizations that could replace losses and employ what remained. This is why the continuing appearance of Soviet armies mattered strategically even when their immediate performance was poor.[2]

A formation can survive its label

An army headquarters might classify an enemy division as destroyed even though groups of its soldiers escaped, while the Soviet system might retain or rebuild the division's designation. Neither practice supplies a complete count of people or usable equipment. The 8 July German table is evidence of German knowledge and confidence, not a census of Soviet survivors.[1]

Occupation was already changing the meaning of defeat

For people behind the front, the invasion's results were not measured primarily in the distance to Smolensk. The opening period had already brought killings of Jews and other civilians, the execution threat to captured political officers, and the expanding imprisonment of Soviet soldiers. The preceding studies have treated Białystok, Kaunas, Lwów and Iași as particular events with particular perpetrators. Their cumulative importance is that violence against civilians was developing alongside the military advance, not waiting for the campaign to end or for a settled civilian occupation administration to arrive.

The persecution in Kaunas had also developed beyond the street violence described in the 25 June study. At the Seventh Fort, a detention site administered by the Lithuanian provisional government under joint German–Lithuanian control, Jewish prisoners were held without food or water. Women suffered sexual violence and murder; men were taken out in groups and shot. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum identifies German SS and policemen and Lithuanian police guards among the perpetrators, and places the culmination of the shootings on the night of 6–7 July. Its estimate of about 5,000 Jewish men murdered covers 30 June–7 July. This was a further stage of persecution within the opening campaign: arrests concentrated people in a guarded site where deprivation, abuse and organized shooting could proceed together.[10]

A written directive from Reinhard Heydrich on 2 July provides another contemporary point of reference. Sent to Higher SS and Police Leaders, it summarized instructions for the Security Police and SD's operational groups. It listed categories marked for execution, including Communist officials and Jews in party and state employment. The wording combined ideological and racial identification with purported security requirements. This was administrative preparation for murder, issued while German headquarters was discussing how rapidly the remaining military resistance could be overcome.[11]

The directive’s wording alone cannot establish that a comprehensive written order to murder every Soviet Jew existed on 2 July. Evidence of the violence actually committed, including the operational groups’ own reports, is needed to trace how the targets and practices of persecution developed. Reading orders and actions together preserves the connection between central authority and local execution without forcing either into a chronology it cannot support. The earlier chapters’ accounts of particular massacres supply the human and institutional specificity that this directive, considered in isolation, lacks.[11][12]

At Drozdy, near Minsk, an inspection on 8 July exposed what captivity already meant. Alex J. Kay’s research identifies the camp as Dulag 127, under the 286th Security Division, and dates the visit by Xaver Dorsch of Organisation Todt, the German construction organization. Dorsch’s report, written on 10 July, described Soviet prisoners of war and civilian detainees crowded into an open field, some without food for six to eight days, with guards firing ruthlessly. The report date falls just beyond this phase; the conditions observed fall within it. These details show lethal deprivation and violence already present in army custody, without projecting the later mass death toll backward into early July. [13]

The Soviet retreat had also exposed crimes committed by Soviet institutions, including the NKVD prison killings discussed in the 1 July study. Establishing those crimes does not transfer responsibility for subsequent pogroms to their Jewish victims or validate Nazi claims of collective guilt. The distinction is both moral and evidentiary: one must identify the agency responsible for each action. The unfolding occupation cannot be understood by granting either dictatorship's propaganda the authority to name innocent people as an enemy deserving punishment.

A victory large enough to be misunderstood

The opening campaign gave German leaders powerful reasons for confidence. They had seized the initiative, disrupted Soviet command, destroyed major formations and carried the war deep beyond the initial frontier. Their armies remained capable of further major operations. The mistake was to treat the scale of those successes as proof that the remaining problem was essentially geographical. Territory still had to be taken, but it would be defended by additional forces generated by a state whose political and administrative structure had survived the first shock.[2][1]

For Soviet soldiers and civilians, the survival of the state offered no immediate relief from the defeats described here. Fresh armies could be committed before their commands were ready; men escaping an encirclement could return to another battle. Yet the continuing formation of those armies changed Germany’s problem. Halder’s confidence rested on destruction already achieved, while the Soviet command was bringing further forces into the line. The next phase begins at that point of contact: the attempt to force the central river defences and destroy a new concentration around Smolensk. [2] [14]

The objective still ahead

Directive No. 21 made the prevention of an organized Soviet retreat into the interior a central requirement. By 9 July, Germany had achieved that purpose against important frontier concentrations and failed to achieve it against all the forces it faced. The surviving armies in the south and the new concentration in the centre gave the next operations their urgency. The relevant test was whether those forces could be destroyed before they sustained a longer war. [15] [1]

The measured verdict is therefore a major German operational victory with the campaign's decisive strategic question still open. Army Group North had reached the Pskov region, the centre was preparing the next struggle around Smolensk, and the south was still trying to bring surviving Soviet armies into an effective encirclement. The Soviet state had suffered a catastrophe and remained in the war. Beyond this atlas's opening phase lay another series of battles in which Germany would seek the final decision that its first eighteen days had made seem close, but had not delivered.

sourceMethod: This conclusion covers events through 9 July. Blau’s German-centred operational reconstruction (printed pp. 44–48) is read alongside Ziemke and Bauer and dated Soviet documents; their numerical assessments are attributed rather than treated as independently audited totals. Soviet records were consulted in published transcriptions. Kay’s scholarly article supplies the 8 July Drozdy inspection, recorded in a 10 July report; later camp mortality is not assigned to this phase. Heydrich’s 2 July instruction was read in Yad Vashem’s published extract. Situation-map symbols remain evidence of German reporting, not comprehensive territorial control. Exact locators and access limitations accompany the review.
